claim: An ultra-high-speed optical trap enabled direct observation of the timing and amplitude of the working stroke, which can occur within <200 μs of actin binding by β-cardiac myosin.
source: An ultra-high-speed optical trap enabled direct observation of the timing and amplitude of the working stroke, which can occur within <200 μs of actin binding by β-cardiac myosin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the ultra-fast force clamp measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: The initial actomyosin state can sustain loads of at least 4.5 pN.
source: The initial actomyosin state can sustain loads of at least 4.5 pN and proceeds directly to the stroke or detaches before releasing ATP hydrolysis products.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements at various force levels up to 4.5 pN.

claim: The initial actomyosin state proceeds directly to the stroke or detaches before releasing ATP hydrolysis products.
source: The initial actomyosin state can sustain loads of at least 4.5 pN and proceeds directly to the stroke or detaches before releasing ATP hydrolysis products.
evidence: This is inferred from the duration and displacement data showing two distinct populations of events.

claim: The rates of actomyosin processes depend on the force.
source: The rates of these processes depend on the force.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the force-dependent rate constants shown in Figure 2f and related analyses.

claim: The time between binding and stroke is unaffected by 10 mM Pi.
source: The time between binding and stroke is unaffected by 10 mM Pi which, along with other findings, indicates the stroke precedes phosphate release.
evidence: This is supported by the ensemble average data in Figure 4 showing similar stroke rates with and without Pi.

claim: The stroke precedes phosphate release.
source: The time between binding and stroke is unaffected by 10 mM Pi which, along with other findings, indicates the stroke precedes phosphate release.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Pi on stroke timing and the observation of Pi-induced reversals.

claim: After Pi release, Pi can rebind enabling reversal of the working stroke.
source: After Pi release, Pi can rebind enabling reversal of the working stroke.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of increased reversals in the presence of 10 mM Pi shown in Figure 5.

claim: Myosin causes displacements of actin filaments connected to work against an external load.
source: In muscle, myosin causes displacements of actin filaments connected to work against an external load.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about muscle contraction.

claim: The majority of the mechanical work done by myosin is performed in the working stroke.
source: The majority of the mechanical work done by myosin is performed in the working stroke, the rotation of the myosin lever arm domain, which occurs soon after actin binding and is closely associated with the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi), a product of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin mechanochemistry.

claim: The working stroke is the rotation of the myosin lever arm domain.
source: The majority of the mechanical work done by myosin is performed in the working stroke, the rotation of the myosin lever arm domain, which occurs soon after actin binding and is closely associated with the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi), a product of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about myosin.

claim: The working stroke occurs soon after actin binding.
source: The majority of the mechanical work done by myosin is performed in the working stroke, the rotation of the myosin lever arm domain, which occurs soon after actin binding and is closely associated with the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi), a product of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing rapid strokes within milliseconds of binding.

claim: The working stroke is closely associated with the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi).
source: The majority of the mechanical work done by myosin is performed in the working stroke, the rotation of the myosin lever arm domain, which occurs soon after actin binding and is closely associated with the release of inorganic phosphate (Pi), a product of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge, though the exact temporal relationship is investigated in this study.

claim: Controversy remains regarding the order of the force-generating conformational transitions.
source: Although substantial physiological and biophysical experiments have provided key details associated with these transitions (Bagshaw and Trentham, 1974; Hibberd and Trentham, 1986; Hibberd et al., 1985; Cooke et al., 1988; Dantzig et al., 1992; Araujo and Walker, 1996; White et al., 1997; Takagi et al., 2006; Muretta et al., 2015; Caremani et al., 2015; Rohde et al., 2017; Llinas et al., 2015), controversy remains regarding the order of the force-generating conformational transitions and whether the free energy change from phosphate release precedes or follows the working stroke (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature showing different interpretations.

claim: Strengthening of the actomyosin bond, tilting of the lever arm, and Pi release all occur within milliseconds of initial actin binding.
source: Strengthening of the actomyosin bond due to conformational changes in myosin and actin, tilting of the lever arm, and Pi release all occur within milliseconds of initial actin binding, making the mechanochemical steps difficult to resolve by commonly available biophysical measurements.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanochemical steps are difficult to resolve by commonly available biophysical measurements.
source: Strengthening of the actomyosin bond due to conformational changes in myosin and actin, tilting of the lever arm, and Pi release all occur within milliseconds of initial actin binding, making the mechanochemical steps difficult to resolve by commonly available biophysical measurements.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal resolution limitations of standard techniques.

claim: The myosin protein was a heavy meromyosin (HMM) construct with a Flag-tag placed at the C-terminus for purification.
source: The myosin protein was a heavy meromyosin (HMM) construct with a Flag-tag placed at the C-terminus for purification.
evidence: This describes the experimental construct used in the study.

claim: The myosin was attached non-specifically to nitrocellulose coated silica beads on the coverslip surface.
source: It was attached non-specifically to nitrocellulose coated silica beads on the coverslip surface.
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: The beta-cardiac isoform is the dominant myosin in the human ventricles.
source: The beta-cardiac isoform not only has great relevance as the dominant myosin in the human ventricles, but its slower kinetic properties compared to fast skeletal myosin facilitated detection of fast rate processes.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: Beta-cardiac myosin has slower kinetic properties compared to fast skeletal myosin.
source: The beta-cardiac isoform not only has great relevance as the dominant myosin in the human ventricles, but its slower kinetic properties compared to fast skeletal myosin facilitated detection of fast rate processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin isoforms.

claim: The slower kinetic properties of beta-cardiac myosin facilitated detection of fast rate processes.
source: The beta-cardiac isoform not only has great relevance as the dominant myosin in the human ventricles, but its slower kinetic properties compared to fast skeletal myosin facilitated detection of fast rate processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design rationale.

claim: Both heads of the HMM construct did not interact simultaneously with actin in the presence of ATP.
source: Although this is a two-headed construct, we did not observe evidence that both heads interacted simultaneously with actin in the presence of ATP (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: UFFC can resolve the onset of actin-myosin binding events to less than 100 microseconds.
source: We employed an ultra-fast force clamp (UFFC) which can resolve the onset of actin-myosin binding events to less than 100 microseconds and filament motions at sub-nm resolution (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the technical capabilities described and cited.

claim: UFFC can detect filament motions at sub-nm resolution.
source: We employed an ultra-fast force clamp (UFFC) which can resolve the onset of actin-myosin binding events to less than 100 microseconds and filament motions at sub-nm resolution (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the technical capabilities described and cited.

claim: Standard optical trapping techniques typically have temporal resolutions > 10 ms.
source: Unlike standard optical trapping techniques which typically have temporal resolutions > 10 ms, UFFC allows observation of the initial myosin working stroke which can occur within 1 ms of actin binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about standard optical trapping techniques.

claim: UFFC allows observation of the initial myosin working stroke which can occur within 1 ms of actin binding.
source: Unlike standard optical trapping techniques which typically have temporal resolutions > 10 ms, UFFC allows observation of the initial myosin working stroke which can occur within 1 ms of actin binding.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: When a surface-attached myosin binds to actin and becomes loaded with the applied force, the filament motion stops within ~50 µs.
source: When a surface-attached myosin binds to actin and becomes loaded with the applied force, the filament motion stops within ~50 µs (Figure 1d–g).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The distributions of event durations span a range from less than 1 ms to greater than 1 s under both assisting and hindering loads.
source: Under both assisting and hindering loads, the distributions of event durations span a range from less than 1 ms to greater than 1 s (Figure 2a–e).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Actomyosin events with durations less than 10 ms represent up to 50% of the observed interactions.
source: The actomyosin events with durations less than 10 ms, which represent up to 50% of the observed interactions, have not been observed previously with standard optical trapping techniques because their durations are below the minimum detectable length (deadtime, 10 ms for standard techniques, 0.5–2.7 ms for the current technique) (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is quantified from the experimental data.

claim: Events with durations less than 10 ms have not been observed previously with standard optical trapping techniques.
source: The actomyosin events with durations less than 10 ms, which represent up to 50% of the observed interactions, have not been observed previously with standard optical trapping techniques because their durations are below the minimum detectable length (deadtime, 10 ms for standard techniques, 0.5–2.7 ms for the current technique) (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of temporal resolutions.

claim: The deadtime for standard optical trapping techniques is 10 ms.
source: The actomyosin events with durations less than 10 ms, which represent up to 50% of the observed interactions, have not been observed previously with standard optical trapping techniques because their durations are below the minimum detectable length (deadtime, 10 ms for standard techniques, 0.5–2.7 ms for the current technique) (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The deadtime for the current UFFC technique is 0.5–2.7 ms.
source: The actomyosin events with durations less than 10 ms, which represent up to 50% of the observed interactions, have not been observed previously with standard optical trapping techniques because their durations are below the minimum detectable length (deadtime, 10 ms for standard techniques, 0.5–2.7 ms for the current technique) (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is measured from the current experimental setup.

claim: For forces > 2.25 pN, three exponential components were necessary to obtain an adequate fit of event duration distributions.
source: For forces > 2.25 pN, three exponential components were necessary to obtain an adequate fit (Figure 2a and f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is determined from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The distribution of durations observed with lower time-resolution, non-feedback measurements are well-described by a single, slow rate of detachment.
source: This result contrasts with the distribution of durations observed with lower time-resolution, non-feedback measurements performed on the same myosin molecules, which are well-described by a single, slow rate of detachment (grey and black, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of different measurement techniques on the same molecules.

claim: kf increases from 1 × 10³ s⁻¹ at low loads to up to 3–6 × 10³ s⁻¹ with increasing hindering or assisting forces.
source: kf increases from 1 × 103 s−1 at low loads to up to 3–6 × 103 s−1 with increasing hindering or assisting forces.
evidence: This is measured from the fitted rate constants in the experimental data.

claim: Events which detach at kf composed 20–40% (Af) of all observed interactions.
source: Events which detach at kf composed 20–40% (Af) of all observed interactions (Supplementary Figure 1b,d).
evidence: This is quantified from the amplitude of the fitted exponential components.

claim: Events which detach at the intermediate rate make up 10–20% (Aint) of observed interactions.
source: The events which detach at the intermediate rate make up a small fraction of observed interactions (Aint = 10–20%, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and detach at a rate, kint = 102–103 s−1.
evidence: This is quantified from the amplitude of the fitted exponential components.

claim: kint = 10²–10³ s⁻¹.
source: The events which detach at the intermediate rate make up a small fraction of observed interactions (Aint = 10–20%, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and detach at a rate, kint = 102–103 s−1.
evidence: This is measured from the fitted rate constants.

claim: kint has an asymmetric force dependence about zero force, increasing from −3.75 pN to +4.5 pN.
source: This rate has an asymmetric force dependence about zero force, increasing from −3.75 pN to +4.5 pN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the force-dependent analysis of the rate constants.

claim: ks is 6–8 s⁻¹ at 1 μM MgATP.
source: ks, which is 6–8 s-1 at 1 μM MgATP (consistent with the measured ATP binding rate) (Liu et al., 2015; Deacon et al., 2012; Bloemink et al., 2014), increases to 10–70 s−1 in the presence of 1 mM MgATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data and consistent with cited literature.

claim: ks increases to 10–70 s⁻¹ in the presence of 1 mM MgATP.
source: ks, which is 6–8 s-1 at 1 μM MgATP (consistent with the measured ATP binding rate) (Liu et al., 2015; Deacon et al., 2012; Bloemink et al., 2014), increases to 10–70 s−1 in the presence of 1 mM MgATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data.

claim: The observation that ks increases with ATP concentration is consistent with ADP release limiting the detachment rate at saturating ATP.
source: This observation is consistent with ADP release limiting the detachment rate at saturating ATP and indicates this population (As) represents motors that have completed the ATPase cycle (Figure 1a) (Liu et al., 2015; Greenberg et al., 2014; Woody et al., 2018a; Sung et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the ATP concentration dependence and supported by citations.

claim: The population detaching at ks represents motors that have completed the ATPase cycle.
source: This observation is consistent with ADP release limiting the detachment rate at saturating ATP and indicates this population (As) represents motors that have completed the ATPase cycle (Figure 1a) (Liu et al., 2015; Greenberg et al., 2014; Woody et al., 2018a; Sung et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic behavior and supported by citations.

claim: The fast detaching interactions do not become faster when MgATP concentration is raised to 1 mM.
source: These fast detaching interactions do not become faster when MgATP concentration is raised to 1 mM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 3), further supporting the suggestion that they detach before completing the ATPase cycle.
evidence: This is shown by comparing rate constants at different ATP concentrations.

claim: Fast detaching interactions detach before completing the ATPase cycle.
source: These fast detaching interactions do not become faster when MgATP concentration is raised to 1 mM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 3), further supporting the suggestion that they detach before completing the ATPase cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ATP concentration dependence.

claim: Fast detaching states do not undergo a working stroke.
source: As shown below, these states do not undergo a working stroke, and are likely the short-lived states described in the physiological and biochemical literature as 'weak-binding' states (Brenner, 1991; Stein et al., 1984).
evidence: This is shown in the displacement analysis and inferred from comparison to literature.

claim: Fast detaching states are likely the short-lived 'weak-binding' states described in the literature.
source: As shown below, these states do not undergo a working stroke, and are likely the short-lived states described in the physiological and biochemical literature as 'weak-binding' states (Brenner, 1991; Stein et al., 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties observed and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Individual myosin working stroke displacements of 5–10 nm were observed shortly after actin binding.
source: Individual myosin working stroke displacements were observed shortly after the linear motion of the actin stopped when myosin attached (Figure 3a). Upon binding, 5–10 nm displacements were observed in many traces.
evidence: This is directly observed in individual traces.

claim: Displacements were rarely seen in interactions with durations below 5 ms.
source: However, displacements were not readily apparent in all traces, and were rarely seen in interactions with durations below 5 ms (Figure 3a, bottom example).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: Short duration interactions likely represent myosins that detach before producing a working stroke.
source: These short duration interactions likely represent myosins that detach before producing a working stroke (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of displacement in short events.

claim: The sizes of the average displacements were highly force dependent, decreasing with increasing force.
source: The sizes of the average displacements were highly force dependent, decreasing with increasing force (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average data.

claim: At forces > 1.5 pN, interactions with durations < 5 ms showed suppressed displacements.
source: At forces > 1.5 pN interactions with durations < 5 ms showed suppressed displacements (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average analysis.

claim: Average displacement of events > 15 ms decreased linearly with increasing hindering load.
source: Average displacement of events > 15 ms decreased linearly with increasing hindering load (Figure 3e–g).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis of long events.

claim: The stiffness of the myosin motor is estimated to be 2.3 pN/nm or greater.
source: If the load-dependence of displacement for interactions > 15 ms is due to compliance within the myosin, (Dupuis et al., 1997) then we estimate the stiffness of the motor to be 2.3 pN/nm (68% CI, 2.0–2.7 pN/nm) or greater from the linear fit to the data points in Figure 3g.
evidence: This is calculated from the force-displacement relationship.

claim: The estimated stiffness of 2.3 pN/nm is at the upper end of previous estimates.
source: This value is at the upper end of previous estimates (Kaya and Higuchi, 2010; Lewalle et al., 2008).
evidence: This is compared to cited previous measurements.

claim: The myosin working stroke occurs within 5 ms of actin binding without a detectable time lag at forces > 1.5 pN.
source: Strikingly, ensemble averages show that the myosin working stroke occurs within 5 ms of actin binding, without a detectable time lag at forces > 1.5 pN (Figure 3f, Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average analysis.

claim: Estimates of the stroke rate from fits yielded rate constants (kstroke) of 700 to 5,250 s⁻¹.
source: Estimates of the stroke rate from fits of the displacement data to single exponential rise (see Materials and methods) yielded rate constants (kstroke) of 700 to 5,250 s-1, that increase with force from 1.5 pN to 3 pN and then plateau (Figure 4c, blue).
evidence: This is calculated from fitting the ensemble average data.

claim: kstroke increases with force from 1.5 pN to 3 pN and then plateaus.
source: Estimates of the stroke rate from fits of the displacement data to single exponential rise (see Materials and methods) yielded rate constants (kstroke) of 700 to 5,250 s-1, that increase with force from 1.5 pN to 3 pN and then plateau (Figure 4c, blue).
evidence: This is observed in the fitted rate constants.

claim: The observed stroke rate constants are likely the sum of the rate for proceeding forward (performing the stroke) and rate for reversing actomyosin attachment.
source: These observed rate constants are likely the sum of the rate for proceeding forward (performing the stroke, Figure 1a, k+5) and rate for reversing actomyosin attachment (Figure 1a, k-4, Supplementary file 1 Table 2).
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic theory.

claim: Only events in which the stroke is faster than myosin detachment are detected and can contribute to the stroke rate in the ensemble average.
source: In fact, only events in which the stroke is faster than myosin detachment are detected and thus can contribute to the stroke rate in the ensemble average.
evidence: This is inferred from the measurement method.

claim: Faster strokes are selected as the detachment rate kf increases with force.
source: Therefore, faster strokes are selected as the detachment rate kf increases with force.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic competition between stroke and detachment.

claim: A slower 1–1.5 nm further displacement was completed in 50–100 ms.
source: A slower 1–1.5 nm further displacement (Figure 3b,e) observed in the ensemble averages was completed in 50–100 ms.
evidence: This is observed in the ensemble average data.

claim: The slower displacement is consistent with the second phase of the myosin working stroke, previously associated with ADP release.
source: The amplitude and time-scale of this slower displacement are consistent with the second phase of the myosin working stroke, previously associated with ADP release (Greenberg et al., 2014; Woody et al., 2018a; Capitanio et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to cited previous observations.

claim: Adding phosphate to contracting demembranated muscle fibers results in a decrease in active force due to the redistribution of myosin states.
source: The addition of phosphate to contracting demembranated muscle fibers results in a decrease in active force due to the redistribution of myosin states (Hibberd et al., 1985; Cooke et al., 1988; Araujo and Walker, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited muscle fiber experiments.

claim: Adding 10 mM phosphate did not substantially change the rates of kf or kint over the range of probed forces.
source: Adding phosphate did not substantially change the rates of the kf or kint over the range of probed forces (Figure 2f, open red and green symbols);
evidence: This is shown by comparing rate constants with and without Pi.

claim: The combined amplitudes (Af+Aint) increased in 10 mM Pi at loads < 3 pN.
source: however, their combined amplitudes (Af+Aint) increased in 10 mM Pi at loads < 3 pN, suggesting an increase in the fraction of events that detach from weak-binding states (Figure 2b,c,g,h).
evidence: This is quantified from the amplitude analysis.

claim: The increase in Af+Aint with Pi suggests an increase in the fraction of events that detach from weak-binding states.
source: however, their combined amplitudes (Af+Aint) increased in 10 mM Pi at loads < 3 pN, suggesting an increase in the fraction of events that detach from weak-binding states (Figure 2b,c,g,h).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of Pi on the amplitude distribution.

claim: There is up to a 50% increase in the number of rapid detachments with 10 mM Pi compared to 0 Pi.
source: The ratio of Af+Aint at 10 mM Pi to Af+Aint at 0 Pi shows there is up to a 50% increase in the number of these rapid detachments (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is calculated from the amplitude ratios.

claim: ks decreased about two-fold at 10 mM Pi and 1 μM MgATP.
source: ks decreased about two-fold at 10 mM Pi and 1 μM MgATP (Figure 2f) in both the UFFC and non-feedback experiments, which is consistent with weak competition between Pi and ATP for binding at the active site, as previously proposed (Amrute-Nayak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is measured from the rate constant analysis.

claim: The decrease in ks with Pi is consistent with weak competition between Pi and ATP for binding at the active site.
source: ks decreased about two-fold at 10 mM Pi and 1 μM MgATP (Figure 2f) in both the UFFC and non-feedback experiments, which is consistent with weak competition between Pi and ATP for binding at the active site, as previously proposed (Amrute-Nayak et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect and supported by citation.

claim: The presence of 10 mM free Pi did not affect the rates of the ensemble displacements for events longer than 25 ms.
source: The presence of 10 mM free Pi did not affect the rates of the ensemble displacements for events longer than 25 ms (Figure 4b and Figure 4c (red)).
evidence: This is shown by comparing stroke rates with and without Pi.

claim: The lack of effect of Pi on stroke rate strongly implicates a mechanism in which Pi release occurs after the working stroke.
source: This result strongly implicates a mechanism in which Pi release occurs after the working stroke, as a delay in the stroke kinetics would have been observed with 10 mM Pi if Pi release and rebinding occurred before the working stroke. (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Pi effect on stroke timing.

claim: The average stroke rate is greater than or equal to the fastest phase of detachments (kf).
source: Comparing the rate of the stroke to the fastest rate of detachment, kf, from the event duration data (Supplementary file 1 Table 2), shows that the average stroke rate is greater than or equal to the fastest phase of detachments.
evidence: This is shown by comparing the two rate constants.

claim: Molecules in the earliest state resolved either perform a stroke or detach, and Pi release does not occur between attachment and the stroke.
source: This result implies that molecules in the earliest state resolved in our experiment either perform a stroke or detach, and that Pi release (or any other substantial intermediate step) does not occur between attachment and the stroke.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of stroke and detachment rates.

claim: Many individual displacement records acquired in the presence of 10 mM Pi showed reversals in the working stroke to the pre-stroke level.
source: Many individual displacement records acquired in the presence of 10 mM Pi showed reversals in the working stroke to the pre-stroke level (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is observed in individual traces.

claim: The average displacement traces decreased after the peak of the initial working stroke in the presence of 10 mM Pi.
source: The average displacement traces decreased after the peak of the initial working stroke in the presence of 10 mM Pi (Figure 5c, dark colors).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average data.

claim: Total displacement was reduced by Pi at all forces above 1.5 pN hindering load.
source: Total displacement was reduced (Figure 5d), and the size of the dip was increased by Pi at all forces above 1.5 pN hindering load (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is quantified from the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The size of the dip was increased by Pi at all forces above 1.5 pN hindering load.
source: Total displacement was reduced (Figure 5d), and the size of the dip was increased by Pi at all forces above 1.5 pN hindering load (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is quantified from the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The changes in total displacement and the amplitude of dip are both greater at higher hindering loads.
source: The changes in total displacement and the amplitude of dip are both greater at higher hindering loads, and the time to reach the minimum of this dip is considerably increased by the presence of 10 mM Pi (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is shown in the force-dependent analysis.

claim: The time to reach the minimum of the dip is considerably increased by the presence of 10 mM Pi.
source: The changes in total displacement and the amplitude of dip are both greater at higher hindering loads, and the time to reach the minimum of this dip is considerably increased by the presence of 10 mM Pi (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is quantified from the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The results are consistent with a model in which Pi is released after the working stroke and then may rebind and cause reversal of the stroke.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which Pi is released after the working stroke and then may rebind and cause reversal of the stroke (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the Pi effects on displacement dynamics.

claim: Simulations of individual actomyosin interactions using a kinetic model with Pi release after stroke recapitulate the observed effects of Pi.
source: We performed simulations of individual actomyosin interactions using a kinetic model with these features (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Ensemble averages of these interactions recapitulate the observed effects of Pi (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: This is shown by the modeling results matching experimental data.

claim: The UFFC system allowed resolution of a short-lived state that is capable of bearing loads up to 4.5 pN.
source: The time resolution afforded by the UFFC system has allowed us to gain novel insights into dynamics of the cardiac myosin initial states following actin attachment and the working stroke. We resolved a short-lived state that is capable of bearing loads up to 4.5 pN and obtained the first estimates of the delay between myosin attachment to actin and the working stroke as a function of applied load from single molecule measurements.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The study obtained the first estimates of the delay between myosin attachment to actin and the working stroke as a function of applied load from single molecule measurements.
source: The time resolution afforded by the UFFC system has allowed us to gain novel insights into dynamics of the cardiac myosin initial states following actin attachment and the working stroke. We resolved a short-lived state that is capable of bearing loads up to 4.5 pN and obtained the first estimates of the delay between myosin attachment to actin and the working stroke as a function of applied load from single molecule measurements.
evidence: This is a summary of the novel findings.

claim: An early actomyosin state that is short-lived but capable of bearing load leads promptly to the working stroke and concomitant strong binding, which is then followed by slower Pi release.
source: Based on the experimental results discussed below, we propose a model (Figure 6) in which an early actomyosin state that is short-lived but nevertheless is capable of bearing load leads promptly to the working stroke and concomitant strong binding, which is then followed by slower Pi release.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The short-lived state detected can stop the motion of an actin filament and maintain forces of up to 4.5 pN for hundreds of microseconds.
source: The short-lived state detected in this study can stop the motion of an actin filament and maintain forces of up to 4.5 pN for hundreds of microseconds.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: The dissociation rate of the short-lived state (kf) is substantially more force dependent under hindering loads as compared to assisting loads.
source: The dissociation rate of the short-lived state found here (kf) is substantially more force dependent under hindering loads as compared to assisting loads (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and as mentioned above it can briefly support loads.
evidence: This is shown in the force-dependent analysis of kf.

claim: The characteristics of the short-lived state suggest that the actomyosin bond in this state is stereo-specific and not a highly disordered interaction.
source: These characteristics suggest that the actomyosin bond in this state is stereo-specific and not a highly disordered interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the force-dependence and load-bearing properties.

claim: The short-lived state's lifetime of ~500 s⁻¹ dissociation rate is fairly close to the measured ~950–1450 s⁻¹ dissociation rate of actomyosin after actin cleft opening induced by ATP binding.
source: The short-lived states we observed are estimated to dissociate at ~500 s−1 in unloaded conditions, fairly close to the measured ~950–1450 s−1 dissociation rate of actomyosin after actin cleft opening induced by ATP binding (Liu et al., 2015; Deacon et al., 2012; Bloemink et al., 2014).
evidence: This is compared to cited measurements.

claim: The short-lived state's lifetime suggests that myosin is in an open-cleft conformation.
source: Comparing this to the <0.1 s−1 dissociation rates measured for known cleft-closed states (Woody et al., 2018a), our short-lived state's lifetime suggests that myosin is in an open-cleft conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to known cleft-closed state kinetics.

claim: Actin-activated Pi release is dependent on a stereo-specific interaction between actin and myosin.
source: Actin-activated Pi release is dependent on a stereo-specific interaction between actin and myosin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Pi release mechanism.

claim: The short-lived state is likely to be a stereospecific, actin-cleft-open state with Pi bound.
source: Thus, our short-lived state is likely to be a stereospecific, actin-cleft-open state with Pi bound.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic properties and comparison to known states.

claim: The model in Figure 6 which places the working stroke before Pi release is supported by the rapid observed rate of the stroke (kstroke) and the similarity between kstroke and kf.
source: The model in Figure 6 which places the working stroke before Pi release is supported by the rapid observed rate of the stroke (kstroke) and the similarity between kstroke and kf (Figure 4), as well as the observations of increased and delayed reversals in the presence of free Pi (Figure 5), as discussed further below.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of rate constants.

claim: There is no appreciable working stroke during the short-lived interactions when time resolution is optimal (forces > 1.5 pN).
source: Ensemble averages of actin displacement during actomyosin events show that there is no appreciable working stroke during the short-lived interactions when time resolution is optimal (forces > 1.5 pN, Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The working stroke appears to immediately follow the short-lived state.
source: The working stroke appears to immediately follow this short-lived state, as the observed rate of the working stroke (kstroke, diamonds in Figure 4c) is greater than or equal to the rate of detachment from the short-lived state (kf, circles in Figure 4c).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of rates.

claim: kstroke shows an increased rate with larger forces in the direction that should hinder the working stroke.
source: kstroke, surprisingly, shows an increased rate with larger forces in the direction that should hinder the working stroke.
evidence: This is observed in the fitted stroke rates.

claim: If the stroke immediately follows the short-lived state, the increase in kstroke with hindering force can be explained by the slip-bond behavior of kf.
source: If the stroke immediately follows the short-lived state, this result can be readily explained by the slip-bond behavior of kf, as the observed kstroke (≈ k+5 + k-4, Figure 1) should increase when k-4 increases.
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic theory.

claim: If a significant intermediate process occurred between entering the short-lived state and the stroke, it would have to occur at >10,000 s⁻¹ to obtain the observed value of kstroke.
source: If a significant intermediate process, such as Pi release, occurred between entering the short-lived state and the stroke, it would have to occur at >10,000 s−1 to obtain the observed value of kstroke (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by simulation of alternative models.

claim: If Pi release and rebinding were to occur before the stroke, kstroke would be slowed by Pi rebinding when it is present in solution.
source: In addition, if Pi release and rebinding were to occur before the stroke, kstroke would be slowed by Pi rebinding when it is present in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic principles.

claim: Biochemical estimates of the Pi release rate for cardiac myosin in solution range from 11.6 to 17 s⁻¹.
source: Biochemical estimates of the Pi release rate for cardiac myosin in solution range from 11.6 to 17 s−1, (Rohde et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015) which is much slower than the observed stroke rate.
evidence: This is cited from biochemical measurements.

claim: The biochemical Pi release rate is much slower than the observed stroke rate.
source: Biochemical estimates of the Pi release rate for cardiac myosin in solution range from 11.6 to 17 s−1, (Rohde et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015) which is much slower than the observed stroke rate.
evidence: This is compared between biochemical and single-molecule measurements.

claim: If Pi release were to happen before or simultaneously with the stroke at a rate of 17 s⁻¹, less than 0.4–4% of the molecules occupying the short-lived state would produce a stroke.
source: If Pi release were to happen before, or simultaneously with, the stroke at a rate of 17 s−1, less than 0.4–4% (high load to zero load) of the molecules occupying the short-lived state would produce a stroke, the rest detaching at ≥500–5000 s−1.
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic competition.

claim: The event duration data show that >10–40% of interactions proceed through the entire biochemical cycle.
source: The event duration data show that >10–40% (high - low load) of interactions proceed through the entire biochemical cycle (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is quantified from the amplitude analysis.

claim: The comparison of predicted vs. observed fractions supports models in which Pi is released after the working stroke.
source: This comparison thus again supports models in which Pi is released after the working stroke and prevents reversal of the stroke and cleft re-opening unless Pi rebinds.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic analysis.

claim: It has been previously suggested that the myosin actin-binding cleft closure and a corresponding increase in actin affinity is tightly coupled to the working stroke.
source: It has been previously suggested that the myosin actin-binding cleft closure, and a corresponding increase in actin affinity, is tightly coupled to the working stroke (Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Málnási-Csizmadia and Kovács, 2010; Xu and Root, 2000), and our data support this hypothesis.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The data support the hypothesis that cleft closure is tightly coupled to the working stroke.
source: It has been previously suggested that the myosin actin-binding cleft closure, and a corresponding increase in actin affinity, is tightly coupled to the working stroke (Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Málnási-Csizmadia and Kovács, 2010; Xu and Root, 2000), and our data support this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that short-lived events show no displacement.

claim: If the binding interface cleft remained open after the stroke, a significant fraction of short-lived events would be expected to show a displacement of actin.
source: If the binding interface cleft remained open after the stroke, a significant fraction of short-lived events would be expected to show a displacement of actin.
evidence: This is inferred from the expected behavior if cleft closure were uncoupled from stroke.

claim: Under conditions when the time resolution was optimal (forces ≥ 3 pN), negligible displacement was observed in short-lived events.
source: Under conditions when the time resolution was optimal (forces ≥ 3 pN), negligible displacement was observed in short-lived events.
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The data provide evidence that the working stroke and cleft closure are both reversible.
source: The data provide evidence that the working stroke and cleft closure are both reversible.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reversals.

claim: The kint detachment rate without added Pi showed an asymmetric force dependence about zero load, consistent with a force-dependent rate for the reversal of the working stroke followed immediately by detachment.
source: The kint detachment rate without added Pi showed an asymmetric force dependence about zero load (Figure 2f, green, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with a force-dependent rate for the reversal of the working stroke followed immediately by detachment from the short-lived, pre-stroke state.
evidence: This is inferred from the force-dependence pattern.

claim: Evidence of stroke reversals appeared in the ensemble averages of displacement as a dip that occurred within a few milliseconds after the initial stroke.
source: Evidence of these reversals appeared in the ensemble averages of displacement both with and without free Pi (Figure 3c,e and Figure 5b,c) as a dip in the displacement that occurred within a few milliseconds after the initial stroke.
evidence: This is observed in the ensemble average data.

claim: An increase in the fraction of rapidly detaching events was observed with 10 mM added Pi at low forces.
source: An increase in the fraction of rapidly detaching events was observed with 10 mM added Pi at low forces (Figure 2g,h).
evidence: This is quantified from the amplitude analysis.

claim: The increase in rapid detachments with Pi is consistent with previous single molecule observations.
source: This result is consistent with previous single molecule observations (Baker et al., 2002; Debold et al., 2013), and with the scheme of Figure 6 in which Pi rebinding allows more stroke reversals which can lead to premature detachments.
evidence: This is compared to cited previous observations.

claim: At higher forces, the increased fraction of direct detachments from the short-lived state may mask the effects of Pi on attachment durations.
source: At higher forces, it is likely that the increased fraction of direct detachments from the short-lived state (at rate kf) may mask the effects of Pi on attachment durations.
evidence: This is inferred from the force-dependent behavior.

claim: Ensemble averages of long events show that added Pi leads to a larger and more delayed dip in the displacement.
source: Ensemble averages of the long events (>25 ms) show that added Pi leads to a larger and more delayed dip in the displacement (Figure 5c-f), consistent with the scheme of Figure 6 in which Pi rebinding allows reversals to occur both more often and later in the attachment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the ensemble average analysis.

claim: The decreased displacement in the presence of 10 mM Pi compared to control is consistent with myosin detaching from a pre-stroke conformation after a delayed reversal of the working stroke.
source: The decreased displacement in the presence of 10 mM Pi compared to control (Figure 5d) is consistent with myosin detaching from a pre-stroke conformation after a delayed reversal of the working stroke.
evidence: This is inferred from the displacement analysis.

claim: For the model to describe the ensemble average data, the lifetime of the pre-stroke state following a reversal was approximately 1 ms under load.
source: It should be noted that for this model to describe the ensemble average data (Figure 5g,h), the lifetime of the pre-stroke state following a reversal was approximately 1 ms under load (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is determined from the modeling parameters.

claim: The lifetime of the pre-stroke state following reversal (1 ms) is longer than the estimated 300 μs lifetime of the initial pre-stroke state under load.
source: This is longer than the estimated 300 μs lifetime of the initial pre-stroke state under load.
evidence: This is compared between different states in the model.

claim: After Pi is released, Pi rebinding may not cause the actin cleft to reopen fully, even if it does allow power stroke reversal.
source: This might suggest that after Pi is released, the Pi rebinding does not cause the actin cleft to reopen fully, even if it does allow power stroke reversal.
evidence: This is speculated based on the different lifetimes.

claim: It has been suggested previously that Pi rebinding may induce transitions off of the canonical pathway.
source: Additional studies and modeling will be required to test this speculation, but it has been suggested previously that Pi rebinding may induce transitions off of the canonical pathway (Debold et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The model in Figure 6 can explain all the observations.
source: The model in Figure 6 can explain all our observations.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the proposed model.

claim: In the proposed model, electrostatically mediated interactions between actin and myosin transition to the short-lived, stereo-specific state.
source: In this model, electrostatically mediated interactions between actin and myosin transition to the short-lived, stereo-specific state detected in our study.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: In the short-lived state, myosin can briefly bear force with an open actin binding cleft and Pi bound.
source: In this state, myosin can briefly bear force with an open actin binding cleft and Pi bound.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the data.

claim: The working stroke of myosin occurs directly from the short-lived state.
source: The working stroke of myosin occurs directly from this state and the closure of the cleft is tightly coupled to the stroke.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: The closure of the cleft is tightly coupled to the stroke.
source: The working stroke of myosin occurs directly from this state and the closure of the cleft is tightly coupled to the stroke.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Both the stroke and cleft-closure can be reversed under zero load, with a rate (kint) that increases with hindering load.
source: Both the stroke and cleft-closure can be reversed under zero load, with a rate (kint) that increases with hindering load.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the data.

claim: Phosphate release occurs after the stroke.
source: Phosphate release occurs after the stroke and rebinding of phosphate allows reversals of the stroke.
evidence: This is the key conclusion of the proposed model.

claim: Rebinding of phosphate allows reversals of the stroke.
source: Phosphate release occurs after the stroke and rebinding of phosphate allows reversals of the stroke.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on Pi effects.

claim: The scheme of Figure 6 is fully consistent with a previously proposed model developed from muscle fiber experiments for skeletal myosin II.
source: The scheme of Figure 6 is fully consistent with a previously proposed model developed from muscle fiber experiments for skeletal myosin II (Dantzig et al., 1992; Walker et al., 1992).
evidence: This is compared to cited previous models.

claim: The previous model for skeletal myosin included a force bearing state followed by reversible force generation and then phosphate release.
source: That model included a force bearing state followed by reversible force generation (the working stroke) and then phosphate release (Dantzig et al., 1992).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Similar studies on cardiac fibers showed the model also applies to cardiac myosin.
source: Similar studies on cardiac fibers showed this model also is applicable to cardiac myosin (Araujo and Walker, 1996).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Recent studies using FRET probes found evidence of a conformational change in the motor domain that precedes phosphate release in skeletal and cardiac myosin II, and myosin V.
source: More recent studies of the rate of the working stroke in skeletal (Muretta et al., 2015) and cardiac (Rohde et al., 2017) myosin II, and myosin V (Trivedi et al., 2015) using FRET probes and time-resolved fluorescence have found evidence of a conformational change in the motor domain, likely a rotation of the lever arm, that precedes phosphate release.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: Previous experiments on fast-skeletal myosin with the UFFC system support that the model of Figure 6 also applies to this myosin isoform.
source: The data from previous experiments on fast-skeletal myosin with the UFFC system support that the model of Figure 6 also applies to this myosin isoform (Capitanio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The present data provide the most direct evidence for the ordering of events after actin attachment in cardiac muscle myosin.
source: The present data provide the most direct evidence for this ordering of events after actin attachment in cardiac muscle myosin.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: High resolution crystal structures of myosin have been used to suggest that phosphate must be released before the stroke occurs.
source: High resolution crystal structures of myosin have been used to suggest that phosphate must be released before the stroke occurs (Llinas et al., 2015; Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from structural studies.

claim: Some models of contraction developed to explain muscle fiber data have suggested that phosphate release and the working stroke are not tightly coupled.
source: In addition, some models of contraction developed to explain a wide variety of muscle fiber data have suggested that phosphate release and the working stroke are not tightly coupled (Caremani et al., 2015; Caremani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous modeling studies.

claim: The data cannot exclude that Pi may occasionally be released before the stroke.
source: While our data cannot exclude that Pi may occasionally be released before the stroke, if this occurred more than 20% of the time, there would be a discernable delay in the stroke rate in the presence of Pi which was not observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Pi effect on stroke rate.

claim: If Pi release before stroke occurred more than 20% of the time, there would be a discernable delay in the stroke rate in the presence of Pi.
source: While our data cannot exclude that Pi may occasionally be released before the stroke, if this occurred more than 20% of the time, there would be a discernable delay in the stroke rate in the presence of Pi which was not observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from kinetic analysis.

claim: Other myosin isoforms may proceed through actin binding, the working stroke, and phosphate release with different dynamics or sequences.
source: The possibility remains that other myosin isoforms which exhibit different kinetic properties than muscle myosin, such as non-muscle myosins V and VI, may proceed through actin binding, the working stroke, and phosphate release with different dynamics or even different sequences (Llinas et al., 2015; Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010; Rosenfeld and Lee Sweeney, 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about other myosin isoforms.

claim: Specific experiments on non-muscle myosins are needed to clarify their mechanisms.
source: Specific experiments on those systems are needed to clarify the mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The HMM protein has 1146 residues that include residues 1–1138 of the human MYH7 gene and a FLAG tag on the C-terminus.
source: The HMM protein has 1146 residues that include residues 1–1138 of the human MYH7 gene and a FLAG tag on the C-terminus (res. 1139–1146).
evidence: This describes the protein construct used.

claim: Bound light chains are those that are constitutively expressed in the C2C12 cells (MLC1/MLC3 and rLC2).
source: Bound light chains are those that are constitutively expressed in the C2C12 cells (MLC1/MLC3 and rLC2).
evidence: This describes the light chain composition.

claim: The trap stiffness used was 0.06–0.08 pN/nm.
source: Experiments were performed with trap stiffness 0.06–0.08 pN/nm and 4–5.5 pN pretension applied to the actin dumbbells.
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: 4–5.5 pN pretension was applied to the actin dumbbells.
source: Experiments were performed with trap stiffness 0.06–0.08 pN/nm and 4–5.5 pN pretension applied to the actin dumbbells.
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: The force signals and feedback output signals were digitized at 250 kHz through a 125 kHz anti-aliasing filter.
source: The force signals and feedback output signals to the EODs were digitized at 250 kHz through a 125 kHz anti-aliasing filter in the sum and difference amplifiers for the x- and y-direction difference signals from the photodiode currents.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: A novel real-time drift and slope correction (DSC) system was added to improve stability and accuracy of the force signal.
source: We added a novel real-time drift and slope correction (DSC) system to our UFFC instrument to improve stability and accuracy of the force signal as a result of thermal changes and other variations.
evidence: This describes a technical improvement to the instrument.

claim: The DSC system markedly improved reliability and consistency within and across experiments.
source: This DSC system markedly improved reliability and consistency within and across experiments, reduced the width of the velocity distributions, lowered effective deadtimes, and improved data reliability at lower forces.
evidence: This describes the benefits of the DSC system.
